subject: Re: Flying seabirds in DISTANCE sampling

messages.subject: Re: Flying seabirds in DISTANCE sampling
parts:
Falk et al.,

I have implemented similar protocol to sample flying butterflies. While I
have not tried different protocols in the field, I have simulated line
transect sampling of moving objects. I have contrasted counts (assuming
perfect detection) of objects that cross a plane perpendicular to the
observer (crossing the "beam") vs. counts that include objects within some
area in front of the observer (as in the popular "Pollard walk"). I have
found that counts of moving objects are always somewhat biased (a true
"snapshot" is not possible) and that the magnitude of the bias (it is
always positive) depends on the speed of the objects relative to the
observer. It is a positive, but nonlinear relationship. Furthermore, the
"perpendicular plane" protocol is much less sensitive to object speed and
generally suffers from less bias.

One problem that I anticipate, and could possibly be addressed in this
forum, is that counting (and measuring distances) only when and object
comes "abeam" may result in excessive heterogeneity in detection
probabilty. That is, one may first detect an object at a close distance
and follow it until it crosses the beam and some greater distance. Its
detection probability is surely greater that objects that were first
detected at the recorded distance.

It seems to me that transect sampling of moving objects is an area in which
not enough attention has been paid. I can't wait to hear more...

~ Aaron Ellingson
